title: Faith, Vows, and Practice
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Faith, vows, and practice are the three essential elements of rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; like the three legs of a tripod, none can be dispensed with. On this, Master Ouyi, in his Essential Commentary on the Amitabha Sutra, gave a clear explanation of the meaning of these three and their mutual relations (see the Annotated Essential Commentary on the Amitabha Sutra):

inline.s: Faith, vows, and practice are the three essential elements of rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; like the three legs of a tripod, none can be dispensed with. On this, Master Ouyi, in his Essential Commentary on the Amitabha Sutra, gave a clear explanation of the meaning of these three and their mutual relations
(see
the Annotated Essential Commentary on the Amitabha Sutra

“The aim (zong) is the essential path of practice, the pivot for meeting the essence, and the guiding principle of all practices.... This sutra takes faith, vows, and name-holding as the essential aim of its practice
(this sutra takes faith, vows, and name-holding as the essential path of practice)

. Without faith, vows cannot be aroused; without vows, practice cannot be guided; without the wondrous practice of name-holding, one cannot fulfill one's vows and realize one's faith. The sutra first presents the environment and personal rewards to give rise to faith, then urges the making of vows to guide practice, then shows name-holding as the way to ascend directly to non-retrogression. Faith means faith in self and faith in others, faith in cause and faith in effect, faith in the phenomenal and faith in the noumenal; vows mean renouncing Sahā and joyfully seeking the Land of Bliss; practice means holding fast to the name with a single, undivided mind.”

“Faith, vows, and name-holding are the essential import of the entire sutra. Faith and vows are the practice of wisdom; name-holding is the practice of deeds. Whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on whether one has faith and vows; the grade of one's station depends entirely on the depth of one's name-holding. Thus the practice of wisdom is the forerunner and the practice of deeds is the principal cultivation, like the eyes and the feet working together.”
Therefore the three provisions of faith, vows, and practice are the core of Pure Land study. The three are an indivisible whole, linked link by link, and their mutual relation is:
with faith arouse the vows, with the vows guide the practice; with practice fulfill the vows, with practice realize the faith.
These sixteen characters are the basic guiding principle of Pure Land study.

That is to say, faith and vows must be carried out in practice before they are true faith and earnest vows; and practice is the actual activity that realizes faith and fulfills the vows, while also being the yardstick for measuring how true the faith is and how earnest the vows are. Those who recite the Buddha's name must possess true faith and earnest vows, and practice according to the scriptural teachings, as the Buddha instructed.

Question: The passage above says: “Whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on whether one has faith and vows; the grade of one's station depends entirely on the depth of one's name-holding.” What does this mean?

Answer: Master Ouyi said: “Faith, vows, and name-holding are the essential import of the entire sutra. Faith and vows are the practice of wisdom; name-holding is the practice of deeds. Whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on whether one has faith and vows; the grade of one's station depends entirely on the depth of one's name-holding. Thus the practice of wisdom is the forerunner and the practice of deeds is the principal cultivation, like the eyes and the feet working together.”

In this passage, “faith, vows, and name-holding are the essential import of the entire sutra” means that faith, vows, and practice (name-holding) are inseparable, being the essential import of this sutra and also the essential path of Pure Land practice. “Faith and vows are the practice of wisdom; name-holding is the practice of deeds” and “thus the practice of wisdom is the forerunner and the practice of deeds is the principal cultivation, like the eyes and the feet working together” mean that faith and vows are the forerunner, like the eyes, while name-holding is the principal cultivation, like the two feet. Without eyes one will wander astray, and without feet one cannot move forward at all. Therefore, viewing “whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on whether one has faith and vows; the grade of one's station depends entirely on the depth of one's name-holding” in its context, the two sentences mean: one who attains rebirth must have faith and vows, and must also have the work of name-holding; one whose work is deep is reborn at a high grade, and one whose work is shallow is reborn at a low grade.
Question: “Whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on whether one has faith and vows” should mean: as long as one has faith and vows, one can attain rebirth.
Answer: To understand it this way raises three problems:

First, if understood this way, then “whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on whether one has faith and vows; the grade of one's station depends entirely on the depth of one's name-holding” would mean: as long as one has faith and vows, one attains rebirth; and as long as one has the work of name-holding, one attains rebirth (deep work, high-grade rebirth; shallow work, low-grade rebirth). In that case, the first half says that as long as one has faith and vows one attains rebirth, while the second half says that as long as one has the work of name-holding one attains rebirth. Then does rebirth depend on having faith and vows alone, or on having the work of name-holding alone? Think — how could Master Ouyi have uttered such a self-contradictory statement?! Therefore one must pay special attention to the difference in meaning between the two phrases “entirely by” (quan you) and “entirely on” (quan ping): “entirely by” denotes a necessary condition (an indispensable condition), while “entirely on” denotes a sufficient condition (the mere possession of this condition is enough).

Second, in this passage of the Essential Commentary, Master Ouyi states very clearly that faith and vows are the forerunner (the one who leads the way) and name-holding is the principal cultivation (the walking). How could it suffice to have only the forerunner without the principal cultivation? Moreover, the Master gives a vivid metaphor: faith and vows are like the eyes, and name-holding is like the feet. Then for a practitioner to reach the destination (the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss), the eyes must watch the road and the feet must walk (eyes and feet working together). How could one reach the destination with only the eyes watching the road while the feet do not walk? This is just as Master Ouyi taught earlier in this Essential Commentary, in the section “Clarifying the Aim”: “The aim is the essential path of practice

. This sutra takes faith, vows, and name-holding as the essential aim of its practice. Without faith, vows cannot be aroused; without vows, practice cannot be guided; without the wondrous practice of name-holding, one cannot fulfill one's vows and realize one's faith.

Faith means faith in self and faith in others, faith in cause and faith in effect, faith in the phenomenal and faith in the noumenal; vows mean renouncing Sahā and joyfully seeking the Land of Bliss; practice means holding fast to the name,
with a single, undivided mind
Third, this passage of Master Ouyi's teaching is:

Before the sentence “whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on whether one has faith and vows; the grade of one's station depends entirely on the depth of one's name-holding” comes “faith and vows are the practice of wisdom; name-holding is the practice of deeds,” and after it comes “thus the practice of wisdom is the forerunner and the practice of deeds is the principal cultivation, like the eyes and the feet working together.” According to your understanding, one would need only the practice of wisdom, the forerunner, the eyes — and could dispense with the practice of deeds, the principal cultivation, the feet — and still reach the destination. How could that be Master Ouyi's original meaning? What is more, Master Ouyi was annotating the Amitabha Sutra; in the sutra, the Buddha teaches that faith, vows, name-holding, and the single, undivided mind can ensure rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. How could Master Ouyi, in his annotation, say that faith and vows alone ensure rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss?
Furthermore, please note: when Master Ouyi explained faith, vows, and practice in the passage above, he pointed out clearly:
“Without the wondrous practice of name-holding, one cannot fulfill one's vows and realize one's faith.... Practice means holding fast to the name with a single, undivided mind.”
He set forth the relation among faith, vows, and practice, and the requirements of practice, with perfect clarity.
The reason Buddha-recitation requires a single mind is that
“the pure mind of Buddha-recitation evokes birth in the Pure Land of the West”
— this is the principle by which Buddha-recitation leads to rebirth.
The original text of this teaching by Master Yinguang is:

“Only when there is a mind-only Pure Land does one gain birth in the Pure Land of the West. If one's own mind is impure, how can one attain rebirth at once? Even those of grave and evil offenses who attain rebirth through ten recitations of the Buddha's name do so because the pure mind of Buddha-recitation evokes birth in the Pure Land of the West.”
(from Master Yinguang's Collected Writings
Answers to Layman Qu Tianxiang's Twenty-seven Questions) He also said:

“To recite the Buddha's name with a scattered mind, one can hardly attain rebirth. This method can bring the mind back to one point; reciting the Buddha's name single-mindedly, one will certainly attain rebirth.”
(from Master Yinguang's Collected Writings
Letter to Layman Chen Xizhou)
Therefore the key to ensuring rebirth is:
true faith, earnest vows, and a single, undivided mind.

This is also the guiding principle of study for those who recite the Buddha's name. Because of true faith, one's vision clearly discerns the scene ahead, seeing both the goal and the road with perfect clarity; because of earnest vows, one's impetus is incomparably powerful, like a river bursting its banks, so overwhelming that nothing can stop it. With true faith and earnest vows, one will certainly follow the World-Honored One's earnest instruction to “practice as taught,” and so bring about the wondrous practice of a single, undivided mind, and through this wondrous practice realize one's faith and fulfill one's vows:
“Now that the mind is single and undivided,
(at the time of death)
then
within, right mindfulness is consolidated; without, the Buddha's welcome is evoked,
and casting off this retribution body, one is at last born in that land.”
(Master Lianchi's Commentary on the Amitabha Sutra)
[So overwhelming that nothing can stop it] Vast and surging, nothing whatsoever can withstand it.
Concerning the relation among true faith, earnest vows, and vigorous practice,
Master Yinguang (the thirteenth patriarch of the Pure Land school)
taught:

“Since you have true faith and earnest vows, you should cultivate the principal practice of Buddha-recitation. With faith and vows as the forerunner, Buddha-recitation is the principal practice. Faith, vows, and practice, these three, are the essential aim of the Buddha-recitation Dharma gate.
To have practice without faith and vows, one cannot attain rebirth; to have faith and vows without practice, one also cannot attain rebirth.
When faith, vows, and practice, these three, are complete and lacking in nothing, rebirth is certain.”
He also said:
“To recite the Buddha's name with a scattered mind, one can hardly attain rebirth.”
(from Master Yinguang's Collected Writings · Letter to Layman Chen Xizhou)
Master Chewu (the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school) said:
“As for those who do not believe, let us set them aside
(those who do not believe — set them aside for the moment and do not speak of them)
. But even among those who believe, to believe without vows is still
(is still)
not to believe. To have vows without practice is still not
(is still not)
to have vows. To practice without vigor is still not
(is still not)

to practice. The reason practice lacks vigor is that the vows are not earnest; the reason the vows are not earnest is that the faith is not true. In short, to give rise to true faith is hard. If faith is truly genuine, the vows will of themselves be earnest; if the vows are truly earnest, the practice will of itself be vigorous. With true and earnest faith and vows, joined to vigorous and diligent practice, one will certainly attain birth in the Pure Land, certainly behold Amitabha, certainly realize the three non-retrogressions, and certainly in a single lifetime fill the position of a Buddha.”
(from the Posthumous Works of Master Chewu)
Master Xing'an (the eleventh patriarch of the Pure Land school) said:
“There are also those who speak of the Pure Land with their mouths while their hearts cling to Sahā; this too is not a true vow. Moreover, the single word ‘vow’ encompasses
(includes)

faith and practice. Faith means that self and other, cause and effect, the phenomenal and the noumenal, are all true (original note: to believe that one's own mind is the Buddha, and that others' minds are likewise; that Buddha-recitation is the cause and rebirth as a Buddha the fruit. The West is the phenomenal; the original nature apart from mind is the noumenal — each is true, hence ‘true’). Practice means to devote oneself exclusively to name-holding, unmixed and unscattered. Vows mean that every thought delights and every moment aspires. Of these three, none may be lacking. There are those who have faith and practice but no vows; but there has never been one who has vows without faith and practice. Question: Suppose someone hears of the Western Pure Land and takes delight in it, yet does not recite the Buddha's name — can he attain rebirth? Answer: If he truly takes delight, he will certainly give rise to aspiration; if he gives rise to aspiration, he will certainly recite the Buddha's name. To delight yet not aspire is certainly not delight; to aspire yet not recite — how can that be aspiration? One who delights, aspires, and recites the Buddha's name and yet fails to attain rebirth has never existed. Question: Suppose someone delights, aspires, and recites, but his worldly mind is heavy and he greedily clings to the dust and toil of the world — can he attain rebirth? Answer: As long as the general is fierce, fear not the strength of the enemy. If his aspiration is truly earnest and his remembrance single-minded, then however heavy his clinging, it will naturally and gradually grow light, and he too will attain rebirth. Like discarding silver to take gold, or discarding fish to take bear's paw — what difficulty is there? Only one fears that the power of the vows cannot match the power of craving, that Buddha-remembrance cannot overcome the thoughts of desire, that one is indolent and heedless, half-believing and half-doubting — then indeed I can do nothing for him.”
(from the Annotated Essay on the Pure Land of the West)
[Only one fears] Means “only one fears.” [Then indeed I can do nothing for him] (For such a person) there is truly nothing I can do. “Mo” means “none.”

Therefore, whether the power of the vows can match the power of craving, and whether Buddha-remembrance can overcome the thoughts of desire — this is the standard by which the genuineness of one's faith and vows is tested.
Question: How can one attain the single, undivided mind of Buddha-recitation?
Answer: The greatest obstacle to attaining the single, undivided mind of Buddha-recitation is the deluded thought. In the practical manual of the “Practice-as-Taught Online Buddhist Academy,”
Aware Buddha-Recitation

, there is a detailed analysis of the causes of deluded thoughts and of how to overcome them effectively; and it explains in detail the concrete steps and methods of study for attaining the single, undivided mind of Buddha-recitation. So long as one has true faith and earnest vows, works hard, advances step by step, and perseveres, one will certainly attain the single, undivided mind of Buddha-recitation.
